title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Money and Dust—The World of Our Mutual Friend

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at one of the strangest and most magnificent novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving through Charles Dickens's last completed novel — chapter by chapter, theme by theme, character by character.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel obsessed with money — where it comes from, what it does to people, and what people will do to get it.
Its opening image is a body dragged from the Thames for profit — and it only gets more unsettling from there.
Today we're beginning with the world Dickens builds — the dust heaps, the fortune hunters, and the extraordinary satirical machinery he deploys against Victorian greed.
I have three brilliant companions for the journey, and I want to introduce each of them properly.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels on audio than arguably anyone alive — he hears Dickens the way a conductor hears a score, every rhythm and rest accounted for.
Oliver, welcome.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who has spent his career understanding the institutions Dickens was attacking — the charities, the courts, the workhouses.
James, it's a pleasure to have you.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite recovered — in the best possible sense.
She cares deeply about what the sentences actually do — on the page and in the ear.
Caroline, delighted you're here.
Let's begin where the novel's energy is centred — with the fortune at the heart of everything, the dust heaps, and the man who inherits them: Nicodemus Boffin, the Golden Dustman.
The thing you have to understand about Our Mutual Friend is that Dickens is writing a novel about rubbish — and he means that quite seriously.
The dust heaps are real — enormous mounds of ash, cinders, and refuse on the edge of London that could make a man spectacularly wealthy.
Old Harmon built his fortune on them, and now his former servant Boffin has inherited the lot.
The moment that news becomes public, Dickens shows us exactly what happens — and it is one of the funniest passages he ever wrote.
He gives us the Secretary sorting through the flood of letters, and what lands first is this:
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
Six words of physical description and you already know exactly what kind of man sent it — and what he wants.
That is Dickens working at full comic speed — the adjectives doing the moral work.
And the Duke of Linseed is not entirely a caricature — that is what makes it sting.
The great Victorian charities absolutely did operate this way — recruiting aristocratic patrons not for their ideas but for their names on a letterhead, and charging them a fee for the privilege.
The comedy Dickens is writing here has a precise legal and institutional target.
He tells us the letter is lithographed — printed by the hundred — and that Boffin's name has been filled in by a different hand.
The Duke has never thought about Nicodemus Boffin for a single moment.
Dickens calls it "friendly" on the Duke's part — and adds, with magnificent deadpan, "and thoughtful in the postscript."
The postscript being, of course, the three-guinea fee.
What strikes me every time I read this section is that Dickens doesn't just satirise the nobility — he moves immediately to the individual beggars, and that shift is devastating.
Because these are people in genuine distress — or claiming to be — and the prose holds both the comedy and the pathos at once.
There is a line about the documents they enclose that I find extraordinary.
"They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
That simile is so peculiar, so specific, and so perfectly right that you have to stop and read it again.
Minced veal to a calf — all the substance has been processed out of it.
And yet it is also quietly grotesque — because a calf didn't choose to become veal.
Caroline has put her finger on something crucial — Dickens keeps sliding the comedy into something darker, and you don't always notice when it happens.
The beggars threatening to be "cold in death" at a quarter to one on Tuesday — with an exact memorandum of the heartless circumstances — that is brilliantly funny.
But behind the joke is the fact that people were writing letters like this.
Dickens received them himself — he was famous and prosperous and the letters came.
He is writing from experience, and the laughter is not entirely comfortable.
And all of this — the dukes, the beggars, the charities — circles around a single legal fact that Dickens sets up with extraordinary care.
The Harmon fortune exists because of a will — a strange, punitive will built by a man with no friends and a rebellious family.
When Wegg reads out the terms of an earlier will he discovers, the language Dickens gives him is both satirical and precise.

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
"Which is quite enough for him" — that aside is extraordinary.
Old Harmon is making a moral judgment from beyond the grave — deciding what someone else deserves, and recording his contempt in a legal instrument.
Wills in Victorian England were exactly that — instruments of control, reward, and punishment — and Dickens understood that better than almost any other novelist.
And that phrase — "rebellious family" — tells you everything about old Harmon without ever describing him directly.
The family rebels because he is a tyrant.
He frames it as their fault, in the very document that proves it is his.
That is the novel's world in miniature — money justifying itself, always, in the language of virtue and desert.
Money, dust, wills, and the language of virtue — we have barely begun, and already the novel is showing us how deeply it intends to dig.
Coming up, we'll look at the river — and the people who live and die beside it.

segments.title: Bella's Gold: Tracing a Woman's Reckoning with Desire

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart, passage by passage, and asks what it's really doing.
I'm your host, and today we're diving into a deep question that runs through the whole book: what does it mean to want money, and what does it cost you?
With me are three people who know this novel with the kind of intimacy that only comes from repeated, loving attention.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic novels than anyone alive — and he hears Dickens as a performer first, catching the rhythms built into the prose.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian whose work puts the novel's institutions — the dust mounds, the bequest, the workhouse — back into the world that made them.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic and lifelong re-reader who has strong views on which characters Dickens treats fairly and which he doesn't.
Let's begin with the novel's comic architecture — because before we can talk about desire and gold, we need to understand the society that worships both.
The thing about Dickens and money is that he never lectures you directly — he builds you a dining room and lets you feel the horror for yourself.
There's a character introduced in the opening pages — Twemlow — and the way Dickens introduces him is, frankly, one of the great comic inventions in English prose.
He calls him, to your face, without apology — listen to this —
"an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint James's, when not in use."
A human being. Introduced as furniture.

And the sustained metaphor that follows — Twemlow as the dining table that gets extended with leaves the more people are invited — is executed with such deadpan relentlessness that you almost forget it's monstrous.
Almost. The punch is in the last detail: the more guests are added, the further Twemlow finds himself from the centre of the table.
What I love about that passage is that it does two things at once — it's genuinely funny, and it's quietly devastating.
Twemlow has a name — he's a cousin to Lord Snigsworth, which is itself a tiny comedy — but Dickens has decided that in this world, lineage without wealth makes you an object.
And the Veneerings, who represent new money with no soul, they use him as social infrastructure.
It sets up everything the novel will interrogate about what money does to people — not abstractly, but very precisely: it decides where you sit at the table.
And that's the landscape Bella Wilfer has to find her way through.
The Veneering world is not satirical exaggeration — or not only that.
The mid-Victorian dinner party was a genuinely elaborate mechanism for sorting and displaying social rank.
Who you could invite, who lent you legitimacy, how the table was arranged — all of it was legible to contemporaries in ways we barely notice now.
So Twemlow's function — cousin to a lord, borrowed for social credibility — that was a real transaction.
What Dickens has done is literalise it with savage precision — turned the social metaphor into a material one.
And once you've seen the furniture metaphor, you can't unsee it when you meet the Boffins — because they represent the exact counter-argument.
The Boffins — the Golden Dustman and his wife — are, for many readers, the emotional heart of this novel.
And Dickens gives them one of the most tender passages in the whole book: Boffin recounting the last time they saw John Harmon as a child.
Oliver, you've read that passage aloud — what does it do to you?
It undoes me, frankly. Every time.
The voice is Boffin's — warm, imprecise, working-class in its rhythms — and Dickens trusts that voice completely.
He doesn't translate it into elegant prose. He gives you the man himself.
The description of the child — seven years old, sent away alone, coming in to warm himself by the fire — Dickens piles detail on detail, each one quietly breaking your heart.
And then he gives you this moment — Mrs Boffin kneeling at the fire, rubbing the boy's cold cheeks, and then the tears:
"she holds him round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, 'I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!'"
That repetition — "wide wide world" — is not an accident.
It's the speech of someone overwhelmed — reaching for language bigger than language can manage.
And the look — Boffin keeps returning to the look the child gives them.
"as if it was in pain — in agony" — that self-correction, that insistence on the stronger word, that's Boffin's grief working in real time.
And then Mrs Boffin waking at night — sobbing, calling out — "Don't you see the poor child's face? O shelter the poor child!"
That's not sentiment. That's trauma, rendered with complete accuracy.
The Boffins carry this child's suffering in their bodies for years. And then the child's fortune falls to them.
Dickens has laid the moral groundwork very carefully.
And that's where the novel becomes almost polemical about virtue and wealth.
Old Harmon — the dead miser — is described in terms that barely stop short of criminal.
Dickens calls him, with magnificent contempt, "the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail."
But even this man — even in his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind — knew the Boffins were different.
Dickens puts it with a kind of cold legal precision — let me find it —
"he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt."
There it is. The miser's ultimate confession: money could not purchase the Boffins.
Which means the novel is arguing, from its foundations, that there exists a form of human integrity that capital simply cannot reach.
And Dickens seals that argument with one of the most perfectly timed lines in the book.
Boffin tells his wife she's a pleasant thing to know — and she had ambitions, brief ones, toward fashionability.
But the moment he says —
"it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!"
— Dickens tells us it was, and I quote, "ruin to Mrs Boffin's aspirations."
"And having so spoken, they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair."
That capital U on Unfashionable. I think about it regularly.
It's Dickens winking at us — and also meaning it completely.
It's a kind of moral comedy — the aspiration punctured at the very moment of its expression.
But what strikes me most in that chapter is that Dickens doesn't punish Mrs Boffin for wanting something more.
He lets the aspiration exist, he lets it be comic, and then he simply shows us what the Boffins actually are — and that's enough.
Compare that to how the novel treats characters who really are captured by money — Charley Hexam, say.
His scene with Bradley Headstone is one of the ugliest things in the book — and I mean that as a compliment.
Charley Hexam is the novel's most ruthless case study in respectability as self-worship.
He has constructed an entire moral universe in which his own advancement is the supreme good.
His sister Lizzie, his teacher Headstone — everyone in his life exists instrumentally.
And when Headstone commits violence — presumably against Eugene Wrayburn — Charley's response is not horror at the act.
It's fury that the act has been inconvenient to him personally.
He tells Headstone —
"you are in all your passions so selfish, and so concentrated upon yourself that you have not bestowed one proper thought on me."
He is accusing Headstone of selfishness. In those words. With no evident self-awareness.
Dickens understood projection long before the word existed in its modern sense.
The comedy of that scene is pitch-black, and the tragedy is that Charley is in some ways the most legible character in the novel.
We recognise him. Entirely. From life.
And the novel is also doing something very interesting with velocity in this section — there's that extraordinary train passage.
It comes at a moment of high tension — and Dickens suddenly pulls the camera back to the railway, crossing London, crossing the river.
Listen to what he does with it —

"the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare."
That syntactic accumulation — clause after clause pressing forward, and then the explosion — it performs the thing it describes.
The sentence is the train.
And then he does something even stranger — he lets the image expand into time itself.
The train becomes a great rocket — "spurning the watery turnings and doublings with ineffable contempt, and going straight to its end, as Father Time goes to his."
The river beneath — with all its living waters, its lights and darknesses, its weeds and flowers — doesn't matter to time.
"for their course has one sure termination, though their sources and devices are many."
In the middle of a plot about gold and inheritance and social ambition, Dickens suddenly opens a door onto eternity.
It's a reminder of what the novel is actually about underneath all of it.
The river runs through all of it — time, desire, money, death.

And what strikes me, listening to this conversation, is how carefully Dickens has laid his moral geometry — the Boffins on one side, Charley Hexam on another, the Veneerings as a kind of satirical backdrop.
The question of what money does to the self — whether it reveals it or corrupts it or simply amplifies what was already there — runs through every relationship in the novel.
We'll be returning to that question in the next segment.
For now — Oliver, James, Caroline — thank you.

segments.title: The Comedy of Pretence: Wit and Disguise in Dickens's Plot

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — and with enormous pleasure.
Each week we take a passage, a theme, a character — and follow it wherever it leads.
Today's subject is one of Dickens's great obsessions: the comedy of pretence — wit, disguise, and the performances people put on to survive, to love, or simply to get through the day.
I'm joined by three guests who have thought hard about this novel and are not afraid to argue about it.

Oliver Trevelyan is an actor, a writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than any living person — he hears this prose the way Dickens himself might have heard it, at a lectern, in front of a crowd.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — he knows what the institutions in this novel actually were, and what it cost real people to live inside them.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite stopped rereading it.
She is, among other things, an expert in which characters deserve better — and will tell you so.
Let's begin at the river, in the dark, with Gaffer Hexam — a man who has very particular views about the company he keeps.
Gaffer Hexam is one of those Dickens characters who arrives fully armed.
He doesn't need a long speech to establish himself — he needs about four sentences and a good contemptuous verb.
And the passage where he dismisses his old partner from the river work is, I think, a tiny masterpiece of comic menace.
He lays out his moral accounting — you got off lightly with the sailors, count your blessings — and then he delivers the verdict.
'We have worked together in time past, but we work together no more in time present nor yet future. Let go. Cast off!'
Those last three words — 'Let go. Cast off!' — they're nautical commands, but they're also just magnificent rage, stripped to the bone.
Dickens is writing for the voice there. You could not misread those three words if you tried.
And the comedy has a social edge that I think is worth pausing on.
Gaffer is essentially performing a moral ejection — he is casting this man out of his professional world on grounds of honour.
The irony being that Gaffer himself trawls corpses from the Thames for profit.
His partner has stolen from a live sailor. Gaffer's entire trade involves the dead.
The hierarchy of criminal scruple here is — well, it is quite something.
Dickens understood that the poor develop very elaborate codes of self-distinction, because when everything else is stripped away, a code of honour is what remains.
What I love about that passage is the rhythm of the accusation — the way Gaffer builds his case like a counsel for the prosecution.
'Make the most of it and think yourself lucky.' It's pure Dickens — the voice of someone who has rehearsed this speech, possibly many times.
But then the dismissal, when it comes, is so terse. Three words. The whole elaborate case collapses into that.
It moves from the comic to something rather colder, rather quickly.
From the river to the drawing room, and to one of the novel's great double acts — the Boffins, and what they endured on behalf of young John Harmon.
James, I know you've been looking closely at the passage where Boffin recounts his battles with Old Harmon.
This passage is extraordinary, because it does two entirely different things at once and neither one undercuts the other.
On the surface, it is comic — Boffin's voice is irresistible, his dialect full of those characteristic Dickensian contractions and malapropisms.
But underneath it, you have a story of a child being systematically brutalised by a wealthy patriarch — and the only protection that child had was two servants.
Boffin sets up his account with characteristic care, and then delivers the detail that makes the whole thing land.

'I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard.'
And then the parenthetical — the black straw bonnet 'perched as a matter of convenience' — that is the comedy doing its work.
It makes you love Mrs Boffin before the blow lands. And then it lands.
'Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.' That repetition is not comedy. That is witness testimony.
James is absolutely right about that repetition.
When I read Boffin aloud, I find myself slowing right down for those last two words — 'Dropped her.' — in a way that has nothing to do with comedy.
There's a stillness in it. Boffin has been building and building — the syntax is rambling, affectionate, digressive — and then it stops.
That is a great writer knowing when to get out of the way of the material.
What moves me about this passage is how much it tells us about the Boffins before the money ever arrives.
They stood out for this child — times out of number, Boffin says — with no legal standing, no power, only decency.
And Mrs Boffin, who takes a bonnet to the temple for a child who isn't even hers, then proposes — once the money does arrive — to adopt an orphan and name him John Harmon.
Dickens gives her the most quietly devastating line for that proposal — let me find it.
'Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him.'
The guilt in that sentence — 'past all benefit of the money' — it's almost unbearable. She knows the fortune has come at a cost she cannot repay.
And of course, what neither the Boffins nor anyone in that scene knows is that John Harmon is not dead at all.
He has assumed a disguise and moved through their lives as the secretary John Rokesmith — and Dickens is entirely open about what he was doing.
James, there's a passage in which Dickens actually addresses the reader directly about the Harmon mystery — almost in his own voice.
It is a remarkable authorial intervention — Dickens steps outside the frame of the novel entirely.
He tells us, quite directly, that he expected a certain class of reader to misread the mystery — and that he found this not alarming but mildly satisfying.
Here is the passage, as he wrote it.

'I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.'
The dry confidence of that sentence — 'I was not alarmed by the anticipation' — is Dickens at his most unapologetically professional.
He is asking his readers to trust the artist's intention — which is itself a kind of performance, a defence of craft.
What I find funny about that passage — and I mean funny in the best sense — is the controlled hauteur of it.
He's essentially saying: yes, some of you thought you were cleverer than me, and I planned for that, and I was fine with it.
And this connects directly to the disguise plot itself — because Harmon as Rokesmith is also performing a kind of patience.
He is watching and waiting to understand who Bella is before he reveals himself — and the moment he finally does is absolutely glorious.
Dickens gives us the narrator describing the scene as if barely able to contain himself.
'My dear, dear girl; my gallant, generous, disinterested, courageous, noble girl!'
Five adjectives in a row — Dickens is parodying the romantic declaration even as he means every word of it.
And then: 'Bella, after hanging her head for a moment, lifted it up and laid it on his breast, as if that were her head's chosen and lasting resting-place.'
'As if that were her head's chosen and lasting resting-place.' That is Dickens writing at the full stretch of his sentiment — and getting away with it entirely.
He earns it, though. That's the thing.
We have watched Bella for so long being vain, being mercenary, arguing with herself — and she does argue with herself, which is what makes her interesting.
By the time she lays her head on his breast, we believe it. We want it.
And then Dickens does something very characteristic — he marks the moment with a meal.
The three of them — Bella, Rokesmith, and dear R. Wilfer — sit down in the counting-house and eat together.
And the narrator reaches for a fairy tale to describe it.

'It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, Somebody's been drinking my milk!'
The hobgoblins without the growlings — happiness as fairy tale with the threat removed.
Even the iron safe of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles stares at them 'like the eyes of some dull dragon' — and for once, the dragon is powerless.
Comedy and tenderness — disguise and revelation — Dickens moves between them without seam, and this novel is perhaps his richest demonstration of that gift.
Oliver Trevelyan, James Blackstone, Caroline Woodcourt — thank you.
We'll be back shortly with more from Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

segments.title: Close Reading: The Boffins' Moral Experiment

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been circling the novel's great mystery — who is John Rokesmith, and what is he really doing in the Boffin household.
Today we go right to the heart of it: the long interior monologue in which John Harmon lays out his entire scheme — why he did it, how it spiralled, and what impossible choice it left him.
Oliver, you've read this passage aloud more than once in your career — I want to start with you on what it feels like as a performance.
It's one of the most peculiar passages Dickens ever wrote — and peculiar is the kindest word I can find.
You have a man essentially conducting a cross-examination of himself — out loud, in his own head, correcting the record as he goes.
Dickens gives him these little courtroom tags — 'Is that so? That is exactly so.' — as though John Harmon doesn't quite trust his own testimony.
And then there's this extraordinary accumulation of guilt and dread in the opening.
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
Three times he says a version of 'mistrustful' — it becomes almost a drumbeat of self-doubt.
As a performer you have to decide: is this a man making excuses, or genuinely confessing?
That question stays with me every time I re-read it.
Because Dickens is very careful, in the chapter that follows, to frame the whole deception through what I can only call structural sympathy.
He writes that Harmon 'lapsed into the condition in which he found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances.'
That phrase — 'accumulative power of its separate circumstances' — is doing a great deal of moral work.
Dickens is asking us to see how a small, well-intentioned lie becomes a trap.
Not through wickedness — through inertia, and fear, and the peculiar paralysis that bad fathers inflict on their children.
And the law would have been absolutely merciless on that inertia, had any of this come to light.
A man known to be alive, allowing himself to be publicly posted as dead on the London walls by the police authorities — that is a serious matter.
It touches on questions of fraud, of inheritance, of the rights of creditors — the Boffins' entire legal position rests on Harmon's supposed death.
What strikes me about the passage is that Harmon himself grasps this perfectly.
He asks himself: 'And shall I come to life to dispossess such people as these?'
He is trapped in a genuinely impossible legal and moral bind — and Dickens renders it with unusual precision for a novelist.
What I love is the moment when the whole scheme is actually born — it's so bathetic, in the best possible way.
He's lying in a pub bed, recovering from a near-murder, and his great moral experiment just — arrives.
Dickens puts it with wonderful precision — listen to this:
'the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
'Of proving Bella.' Two words. After all that elaborate machinery — that's the engine.
And there's something very Dickensian about it — the grand scheme conceived in a rented bed above a public bar.
The sailors' disguise section is where it becomes almost farcical — and Dickens knows it.
He and Radfoot, two men of education who've been to school in Brussels, kit themselves out as common sailors to observe a girl in Holloway.
The passage describes it with this almost conspiratorial glee.
'The plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
'Throwing ourselves in her neighbourhood' — it reads like two overeducated young men playing at adventure.
And yet the reason behind it — the terror of a mercenary marriage, the distrust of his own inheritance — is entirely serious.
That distrust of inherited wealth is one of the novel's genuinely radical threads.
Harmon's father is never exactly a villain — he's more of an absence, a corrupting force that poisons everything he touches from beyond the grave.
The son returns to England knowing of 'nothing but wretchedness that my father's wealth had ever brought about.'
That is not a minor caveat — that is a total indictment of a patrimonial system.
And Dickens wraps that indictment in the comedy of the Boffins — which is where it gets genuinely interesting.
Oh, the Boffins — yes — this is where the novel exhales.
Because after all that dark interior wrestling, Dickens gives us Mr Boffin on the subject of charitable patronage — and it is magnificent.
You have to hear this in full, because the rhythm is everything:

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
Up to his neck in charity solicitations — while he himself is living under a false identity.
The irony is almost structural.
And Boffin's fury is entirely genuine — that's what makes it land.
He's not a satirist performing outrage — he's a man genuinely baffled and offended by pretension.
'If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain't he a Patron, and if Mrs Jack Styles gives her five shillings ain't she a Patroness?'
The names — Tom Noakes, Jack Styles — are so perfectly chosen: they're the most ordinary people in England, suddenly ennobled by a coin.
And next to John Harmon's agonies over wealth and identity, Boffin's cheerful contempt for charitable vanity is — well, it's a kind of moral fresh air.
It's also a very precise satire on how Victorian philanthropy actually worked.
The charitable subscription lists were a form of social advertising — your name, your rank, your donation, all published for the world to see.
Boffin's instinct — that a five-shilling donor shouldn't get the same title as a five-hundred-pound donor — is actually the system working as designed.
The impudence Boffin sees is really the impudence of the entire machinery of social respectability — which is, of course, precisely Dickens's target.
What strikes me, pulling all this together, is how Dickens manages to hold his harshest social critique and his warmest comedy in the same space.
John Harmon's despair about inherited money and Mr Boffin's spluttering rage about charity forms — they're actually interrogating the same question.
What does wealth do to people — and what does it ask of them?
Coming up, we turn to the river — and what Dickens makes of the world that lives and dies by its banks.

segments.title: Class, Consciousness, and the Narrative Mirror

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

We've been circling around the novel's obsession with money and identity, and now we want to press into something sharper — the way Dickens uses appearance, aspiration, and exploitation to map the full architecture of class.
James Blackstone has been sitting on some passages that range from the genuinely tender to the genuinely alarming, and I want to give him the floor first.
Thank you. I want to start somewhere unexpectedly quiet — a rooftop, a carpet, two women reading.
Dickens gives us Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren in one of the most carefully composed pastoral images in the entire novel.
And the narrator frames it with a line that is generous and, if you read it carefully, also complicated.
The passage reads:
"Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren. For whom, perhaps with some old instinct of his race, the gentle Jew had spread a carpet... they both pored over one book; both with attentive faces."
That phrase — 'some old instinct of his race' — is the kind of thing that makes the modern reader flinch, and rightly so.
Dickens means it as praise of Riah, but the framing is racial essentialism, however warmly intended.
What redeems the image — and I think it does redeem it — is the absolute equality with which the two women are placed on that carpet, sharing one book.
That image stays with you precisely because it's so fragile.
They're sitting against a blackened chimney-stack — industry pressing in on all sides — and yet Dickens gives them books, and fruit, and beads.

The small comedy of those chimneys — 'twirling their cowls and fluttering their smoke, rather as if they were bridling, and fanning themselves' — is Dickens giving his industrial landscape social pretensions.
Even the chimneys are putting on airs, looking down on these two poor women who are simply trying to learn.
And notice Dickens's precision — Jenny's face is sharper, Lizzie's more perplexed.
One sentence, and he's told you everything about both women's relationship to knowledge.
I love that you've picked up on the chimneys, because that's pure theatrical Dickens — the world itself becomes a chorus of disapproving onlookers.
But I want to come at class from the opposite direction — from the comic grotesque rather than the tender pastoral.
Because when Dickens wants to show you the cruelty of class through clothing, he doesn't write tragedy. He writes Sloppy.
The tailor has been instructed — by Rokesmith, on Mrs Boffin's behalf — to conceal the buttons.
The novel tells us:
"he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators."
The body refuses to be dressed.
Sloppy's form is more powerful than the entire science of tailoring, and Dickens celebrates that with complete joy.
That passage is funny, but it's also a precise social document.
The whole machinery of charitable dressing-up is there: Mrs Boffin's consideration, Rokesmith's supervision, the tailor's art deployed in the service of concealment.
The Victorian philanthropic impulse often worked exactly like this — trying to make the poor presentable to a middle-class gaze, rather than addressing the conditions that made them poor.
And Sloppy, magnificently, won't stay concealed.
But the passage I find most disturbing — and most revealing about how class operates in this novel — is Wegg's blackmail scheme against Boffin.
Because there, class resentment has curdled into something almost ideological — a logic of extraction masquerading as justice.
Wegg articulates his scheme in this remarkable passage:

"he considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!' ... he should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions."
'Abject moral bondage and slavery' — applied to a man who rose from dustman's fortune to respectability.
Wegg has simply inverted the class logic of his oppressors and called it principle.
What strikes me about that Wegg passage is the prose style itself — all those 'That' clauses, stacked and stacked.
It's parliamentary oratory in the mouth of a wooden-legged ballad-monger, and Dickens is satirising the language of rights and entitlement when deployed for naked greed.
The phrase 'minion of fortune and worm of the hour' is supposed to sound grand, and it does — in the most deflating way imaginable.
Wegg is performing class warfare as rhetoric while being entirely empty of any genuine grievance.
And yet the novel provides the counter-image — because when John Harmon finally confronts Wegg, he has a completely different language for the same moral universe.
Harmon says of Boffin:
"I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin."
That parenthesis — 'there are no words to satisfy me' — is Dickens's honesty about language's limits in the face of genuine virtue.
Wegg has too many words. Harmon has too few. That's the whole moral geometry of the novel in two moments.
That is beautifully put, and I want to add one final image to this gallery — because Dickens gives us one more portrait of a man consumed by his own position in the social order.
Bradley Headstone — the schoolmaster who has clawed his way up from nothing, and is now being dragged back down by Riderhood.
The novel gives him one of the most terrifying physical portraits of despair I've ever read aloud.
Listen to this:

"Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating."
'The very texture and colour of his hair degenerating.' Not greying. Degenerating.
That is a man being literally undone by shame and social terror — by everything he worked to become, collapsing.
Sloppy's buttons gleam with irrepressible life. Bradley's face turns to ash. Class does different things to different bodies in this novel.
A rooftop garden, a suit that refuses to behave, a scheme dressed in parliamentary language, and a man turning to ash by firelight.
Dickens gives the whole range — comic, pastoral, polemical, gothic — but they are all, as Oliver says, portraits of what class does to the human form.
In our next segment, we turn to the river — and what it takes and what it returns.

utterances.text: We've arrived at the final movement of Our Mutual Friend — the place where Dickens ties his knots, some with silk, some with rope.
Endings in this novel are never simple resolutions — they're verdicts.
Some characters are redeemed, some are damned, and at least one is deposited in a refuse cart.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, audiobook veteran, connoisseur of Dickensian justice — I suspect you've been waiting for that refuse cart all episode.
James Blackstone brings his historian's eye to what these endings reveal about power and punishment.
And Caroline Woodcourt — our close reader — will tell us, I'm sure, which characters deserved better and which got exactly what was coming.
Let me say immediately and without apology that the disposal of Silas Wegg is one of the great comic set-pieces in all of Dickens.
Wegg has schemed and wheedled and blackmailed his way through nearly eight hundred pages — and his reward is Sloppy.
Dickens sets up the moment with perfect comic economy — let me read you the whole glorious sentence.
"Sloppy lightly trotted out with him and trotted down the staircase, Mr Venus attending to open the street door.

Mr Sloppy's instructions had been to deposit his burden in the road; but, a scavenger's cart happening to stand unattended at the corner, with its little ladder planted against the wheel, Mr S. found it impossible to resist the temptation of shooting Mr Silas Wegg into the cart's contents.
A somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity, and with a prodigious splash."
A prodigious splash.
That full stop is doing more work than most novelists manage in a chapter.
What kills me every time is "Mr S." — that sudden abbreviation, that little flash of mock-formality right before the splash.
Dickens is almost winking at us.
He's treating Sloppy — this gentle, enormous, much-underestimated young man — with the full dignity of bureaucratic notation.
While Wegg gets shot into a dust cart.
And there's a thematic rightness to it that goes deeper than comedy.
The dust mounds are where Wegg's ambitions were born — his scheme to rob old Harmon's fortune from within the dust.
He returns there. The circle is complete.
The dust economy is central here, and Dickens understood it with documentary precision.
The dust mounds were real — mountains of household and street waste that were sorted and sold, yielding fortunes to those who owned the rights.
Wegg ends where the system's wealth begins — in the filth that generates it.
But the novel is equally precise about the psychology of those who don't get anything as clean as comic humiliation.
Bradley Headstone's fate is described in terms that I find genuinely disturbing — perhaps the darkest passage in the whole book.
Dickens writes that he is, and I want to read this carefully:
"cursed with a state of mind more wearing and more wearisome than remorse.
He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently."
No remorse — but a punishment worse than remorse.
The crime is rehearsed endlessly, improved upon mentally, made perfect — and that mental perfectionism is itself the hell.
It's extraordinary as psychological writing — and it reads like something from a much later century.
Headstone has no arc of redemption, no catharsis, no last-minute grace.
Just the obsessive loop — the crime refined in the mind, over and over.
And what makes it theatrically brilliant is that it's unplayable — you can't show it on stage, you can barely voice it.
It lives entirely on the page, in that relentless Dickensian prose rhythm.
I want to come back to something gentler — and funnier — before we close.
Eugene Wrayburn's account of his father's method of predetermining every child's career is — I find it inexhaustibly delightful.
He refers to his father throughout as M. R. F. — Most Respected Father — which is simultaneously affectionate and completely withering.
And then he delivers the line that I think sums up the whole novel's attitude to inherited destiny:
"When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, 'this,' says M. R. F., 'is a little pillar of the church.'
Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one."
A very shaky one.
The whole social edifice in four words.
That passage captures the complete arbitrariness of how Victorian society allocated its human beings.
Eugene was disposed of as a barrister before he'd drawn breath — and the novel shows us what that disposal costs a man of genuine intelligence.
His brilliant idleness isn't sloth — it's the correct response to a system that never asked him what he wanted.
And Dickens pairs that — fascinatingly — with the passage about another young life wasted by a different kind of predetermination.
Lizzie speaks of a child whose fate was sealed by circumstance rather than parental decree — and Dickens gives us the most devastating parenthesis in the book.
"This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley."
"If she ever had one."
That clause does not shout. It simply opens a void.
When I recorded passages like that one, I found I had to stop after the clause.
Not for effect — genuinely needed a moment.
Because Dickens has been making you laugh for three hundred pages and then he places that parenthesis and there's nothing left to do with it.
It doesn't ask for pity in the sentimental Victorian way — it just states a fact so sparse it becomes unbearable.
That's the dual engine of this novel — comedy and devastation, running simultaneously, neither undercutting the other.
And it's why re-reading it is so different from reading it the first time.
You carry the ending back into the middle, and everything shifts.
Wegg's comic menace becomes pathetic.
Headstone's violence becomes a kind of terrible pre-determined grief.
And Eugene's idleness becomes — almost — a form of integrity.
The novel earns its title. Everyone is, in some sense, our mutual friend — and our mutual problem.
Comedy and devastation, running simultaneously — I don't think I'll find a better summary of Our Mutual Friend than that.
My thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt — three readers whose company I'd choose for any novel, but especially this one.
Our Mutual Friend was Dickens's last completed novel — finished in 1865, just five years before his death.
It rewards every return.
We'll be back with more episodes from the series — until then, thank you for listening to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

c40:p31.text:
‘Exactly so, sir!’ returned Wegg, blandly and buoyantly. ‘I see I take you
      with me! Hear, hear, hear! Resolved, as your discriminating good sense
      perceives, that if you was to have a sap—pur— ize , it should be
      a complete one! Well, sir. And so, as you have honoured me by
      anticipating, I examined the document. Regularly executed, regularly
      witnessed, very short. Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever
      had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the
      Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and
      residue of his property to the Crown.’
c40:p31.summary: Wegg describes the will's contents: John Harmon leaves the Little Mound to Boffin and the remainder to the Crown, having no close relationships.
c40:p31.best_quote: Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.

c2:p2.text:
There was an innocent piece of dinner-furniture that went upon easy
      castors and was kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street, Saint
      James’s, when not in use, to whom the Veneerings were a source of blind
      confusion. The name of this article was Twemlow. Being first cousin to
      Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might
      be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state. Mr and Mrs
      Veneering, for example, arranging a dinner, habitually started with
      Twemlow, and then put leaves in him, or added guests to him. Sometimes,
      the table consisted of Twemlow and half a dozen leaves; sometimes, of
      Twemlow and a dozen leaves; sometimes, Twemlow was pulled out to his
      utmost extent of twenty leaves. Mr and Mrs Veneering on occasions of
      ceremony faced each other in the centre of the board, and thus the
      parallel still held; for, it always happened that the more Twemlow was
      pulled out, the further he found himself from the center, and nearer to
      the sideboard at one end of the room, or the window-curtains at the other.
c2:p2.summary: Twemlow, a man of good family connections, is introduced through an extended metaphor comparing him to a dining table that the Veneerings manipulate for social purposes.
c2:p2.best_quote: Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state.

c8:p43.text:
‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’
c8:p43.summary: Boffin recounts the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon, a seven-year-old being sent to a foreign school, including the poignant moment when Mrs Boffin wept while warming the boy by the fire and embraced him protectively, expressing a desire to save him—a memory that haunted her for years.
c8:p43.best_quote: There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the steamboat... Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come into the child's eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, "I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!"

c9:p30.text:
Through his most inveterate purposes, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail had
      known these two faithful servants to be honest and true. While he raged at
      them and reviled them for opposing him with the speech of the honest and
      true, it had scratched his stony heart, and he had perceived the
      powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to
      the attempt. So, even while he was their griping taskmaster and never gave
      them a good word, he had written their names down in his will. So, even
      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and
      sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself—he
      was as certain that these two people, surviving him, would be trustworthy
      in all things from the greatest to the least, as he was that he must
      surely die.
c9:p30.summary: Dickens explains that old John Harmon, despite his misanthropy and greed, respected the Boffins' moral integrity so deeply that he named them in his will as trustees of his fortune.
c9:p30.best_quote: he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt

c57:p86.text:
‘When I speak of my sister, I devoutly wish that you had never seen her,
      Mr Headstone. However, you did see her, and that’s useless now. I confided
      in you about her. I explained her character to you, and how she interposed
      some ridiculous fanciful notions in the way of our being as respectable as
      I tried for. You fell in love with her, and I favoured you with all my
      might. She could not be induced to favour you, and so we came into
      collision with this Mr Eugene Wrayburn. Now, what have you done? Why, you
      have justified my sister in being firmly set against you from first to
      last, and you have put me in the wrong again! And why have you done it?
      Because, Mr Headstone, you are in all your passions so selfish, and so
      concentrated upon yourself that you have not bestowed one proper thought
      on me.’
c57:p86.summary: Charley recounts how his favor and support for Bradley have been repaid with violence that justifies Lizzie's opposition and damages Charley himself.
c57:p86.best_quote: you are in all your passions so selfish, and so concentrated upon yourself that you have not bestowed one proper thought on me

c61:p86.text:
Then, the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides
      of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and
      under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over
      the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded
      in the rush of smoke and steam and glare. A little more, and again it
      roared across the river, a great rocket: spurning the watery turnings and
      doublings with ineffable contempt, and going straight to its end, as
      Father Time goes to his. To whom it is no matter what living waters run
      high or low, reflect the heavenly lights and darknesses, produce their
      little growth of weeds and flowers, turn here, turn there, are noisy or
      still, are troubled or at rest, for their course has one sure termination,
      though their sources and devices are many.
c61:p86.summary: The train departs the station and travels through London and its suburbs, crossing the river in a magnificent burst of power, metaphorically described as a projectile bursting across the water.
c61:p86.best_quote: the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare.

c1:p43.text:
‘No you won’t. I’ll tell you what it is. You got off with a short time of
      it for putting your hand in the pocket of a sailor, a live sailor. Make
      the most of it and think yourself lucky, but don’t think after that to
      come over  me  with your pardners. We have worked together in time past, but
      we work together no more in time present nor yet future. Let go. Cast
      off!’
c1:p43.summary: Gaffer cuts off the boatman and declares that they will no longer work together, threatening violence if the boatman does not leave.

c8:p39.text:
‘And speaking of satisfactory,’ pursued Mr Boffin, ‘why, Lord save us!
      when we come to take it to pieces, bit by bit, where’s the
      satisfactoriness of the money as yet? When the old man does right the poor
      boy after all, the poor boy gets no good of it. He gets made away with, at
      the moment when he’s lifting (as one may say) the cup and sarser to his
      lips. Mr Lightwood, I will now name to you, that on behalf of the poor
      dear boy, me and Mrs Boffin have stood out against the old man times out
      of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to. I
      have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the
      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top
      of her head), and send it spinning across the yard. I have indeed. And
      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should
      have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn’t thrown herself
      betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr
      Lightwood. Dropped her.’

      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.

On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.

‘Now, scoundrel,’ he pursued, ‘I am going to finish. You supposed me just

      through any act of my father’s, or by any right I have? No. Through the

      possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness,
      goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin. And

      through his clenched teeth, and with a very ugly turn indeed on Wegg’s
      cravat, ‘that I didn’t try to twist your head off, and fling  that  out of

Now, too, was he cursed with a state of mind more wearing and more
      wearisome than remorse. He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold
      that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing
      the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently. In the defensive
      declarations and pretended confessions of murderers, the pursuing shadow
      of this torture may be traced through every lie they tell. If I had done
      it as alleged, is it conceivable that I would have made this and this
      mistake? If I had done it as alleged, should I have left that unguarded
      place which that false and wicked witness against me so infamously deposed
      to? The state of that wretch who continually finds the weak spots in his
      own crime, and strives to strengthen them when it is unchangeable, is a
      state that aggravates the offence by doing the deed a thousand times
      instead of once; but it is a state, too, that tauntingly visits the
      offence upon a sullen unrepentant nature with its heaviest punishment
      every time.
